author: Alex Chen
original_text:
SYNTHETIC DEMO POST — not a real LinkedIn post.

Our agent became more reliable when we treated context as an engineered resource, not a growing transcript. We separated durable instructions, retrieved evidence and temporary tool results. Each tool response now has a token budget and an expiry boundary.

Before every model call, we select only evidence relevant to the current step. We retain source references so reviewers can trace an answer back to its inputs. This is a design sketch, not a published performance benchmark.

insight.title: The next frontier isn't the model. It's the context.
insight.summary: A practical shift from longer prompts to deliberately designed context: scoped evidence, bounded tool output, and traceable decisions.
insight.main_insight: Treat each agent step as a context assembly problem, separating stable instructions from transient evidence.
insight.practical_relevance: Audit what enters each model call. Assign tool outputs explicit budgets and preserve references to the original evidence.
insight.why_it_matters: More context is not always more useful context. Deliberate selection makes agent behavior easier to inspect.

author: Maya Patel
original_text:
SYNTHETIC DEMO POST — not a real LinkedIn post.

A RAG evaluation should separate retrieval misses from generation errors. We maintain a small question set with expected source passages. First, measure whether the retriever returns the passage. Then test whether the answer is supported by it. Chunk size, metadata filters and reranking can each change retrieval behavior; alter one at a time.

insight.title: Your RAG pipeline needs an evaluation loop, not another vector database.
insight.summary: Separate retrieval failures from answer failures before tuning your stack. Start with a small, source-grounded evaluation set.
insight.main_insight: Evaluate retrieval and generation independently to locate failures.
insight.practical_relevance: Build an evaluation set that pairs questions with known source passages.
insight.why_it_matters: Infrastructure changes cannot fix failures you have not isolated.

author: Jordan Ellis
original_text:
SYNTHETIC DEMO POST — not a real LinkedIn post.

For an MCP tool that writes customer records, a valid tool schema is only the first boundary. The server must enforce the calling user's permissions, validate every field and make retries idempotent. Tool descriptions are useful hints, not an authorization system. Require human approval for consequential writes.

insight.title: MCP connects the tools. You still own the trust boundary.
insight.summary: Schema validation is not authorization. Put identity checks, idempotency, and approval boundaries on the server.
insight.main_insight: An agent's ability to describe a tool call is not permission to execute it.
insight.practical_relevance: Review write tools for server-enforced user permissions and safe retries.
insight.why_it_matters: Tool integration increases capability and the importance of explicit trust boundaries.

author: Sam Rivera
original_text:
SYNTHETIC DEMO POST — not a real LinkedIn post.

Before introducing a second agent, write down the artifact it owns and the condition that ends its work. A coordinator should pass explicit inputs and expect a typed result. If the task is a single continuous reasoning trace, splitting it can add coordination cost without improving the outcome.

insight.title: Multi-agent systems work better with fewer, clearer handoffs.
insight.summary: Give each agent a bounded artifact, explicit inputs, and a stopping condition. Don't split a continuous reasoning task just to add agents.
insight.main_insight: Coordination is a cost; isolate work only when it has a clear boundary.
insight.practical_relevance: Define a result schema and stop condition before delegating.
insight.why_it_matters: Explicit boundaries make complex agent workflows easier to debug.
